questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort when the pivot is always the smallest element?
questions.explanation: When the pivot is always the smallest (or largest) element, partitioning yields one subarray of size n−1 and one of size 0, leading to a recurrence T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n), which solves to O(n²).

distractor_rationales.O(n): This would imply linear work total, but quicksort must compare most elements multiple times in this degenerate case.
distractor_rationales.O(n log n): This is the average-case complexity with balanced partitions; it does not hold when pivots consistently yield worst-case splits.
distractor_rationales.O(log n): This is far too optimistic — even reading all input requires Ω(n) time, so no correct comparison-based sort can be sublinear.

questions.prompt: Which collision resolution strategy in hash tables guarantees O(1) worst-case lookup time assuming a perfect hash function and fixed table size?
questions.explanation: With a perfect hash function and fixed table size, separate chaining places at most one key per bucket; thus lookup is O(1) worst-case. Other open-addressing methods may require probing sequences that grow with load.

distractor_rationales.Linear probing: Worst-case lookup can degrade to O(n) due to clustering, even with good hashing.
distractor_rationales.Double hashing: Still subject to long probe sequences under high load or adversarial inputs; worst-case is not bounded by constant time.
distractor_rationales.Open addressing with cuckoo hashing: Cuckoo hashing offers O(1) *amortized* lookup, but worst-case lookup is O(log n) due to relocation chains during insertion; lookup itself is O(1), but guarantee depends on implementation assumptions — separate chaining is simpler and unambiguously O(1) worst-case here.

questions.prompt: In a valid binary search tree (BST), which property must hold for every node?
choices: The left subtree contains only nodes with keys less than the node's key
The right subtree contains only nodes with keys greater than or equal to the node's key
The height of left and right subtrees differs by at most one
The node's key is the median of all keys in its subtree
questions.correct_answer: The left subtree contains only nodes with keys less than the node's key
questions.explanation: By definition, a BST requires that for every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly less than the node’s key, and all keys in the right subtree are strictly greater.

distractor_rationales.The right subtree contains only nodes wi: BSTs require strict inequality on both sides; allowing equality violates uniqueness and ordering guarantees.
distractor_rationales.The height of left and right subtrees di: This describes an AVL tree (a self-balancing BST), not a general BST.
distractor_rationales.The node's key is the median of all keys: A BST does not enforce median placement; e.g., a right-skewed tree satisfies BST property without medians.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is most appropriate for finding the shortest path from a single source to all other vertices in a weighted, directed graph with negative edge weights but no negative cycles?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles; it computes shortest paths from a single source in O(VE) time.

distractor_rationales.Dijkstra's algorithm: It assumes non-negative edge weights; with negatives, it may produce incorrect results due to premature finalization of distances.
distractor_rationales.Floyd-Warshall algorithm: It solves the all-pairs shortest paths problem, not single-source — overkill and less efficient (O(V³)) for this use case.
distractor_rationales.Prim's algorithm: This is for minimum spanning trees in undirected graphs, not shortest paths.

questions.prompt: What is the primary distinguishing feature of problems suitable for dynamic programming?
choices: They can be solved recursively with overlapping subproblems
They involve greedy choices that lead to global optimality
They require backtracking to explore exponential solution spaces
They must be formulated as linear programs
questions.correct_answer: They can be solved recursively with overlapping subproblems
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming exploits optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems — computing each subproblem once and reusing solutions via memoization or tabulation.

distractor_rationales.They involve greedy choices that lead to: That defines greedy algorithms, not DP; greedy methods don’t revisit or reuse subproblem solutions.
distractor_rationales.They require backtracking to explore exp: Backtracking explores all possibilities without reuse; DP avoids recomputation precisely to avoid exponential blowup.
distractor_rationales.They must be formulated as linear progra: LP is a different paradigm; many DP problems (e.g., knapsack) are integer/nonlinear and not naturally LP-formulated.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap implemented as an array, where is the largest element always located?
questions.explanation: By definition, in a max-heap, the root (largest element) is stored at index 0 in the array representation, with children at indices 2i+1 and 2i+2.

distractor_rationales.At the last index: The last index holds a leaf node, which could be minimal — no heap invariant constrains leaf values.
distractor_rationales.At index ⌊n/2⌋: This is the index of the first leaf node (in 0-based array), not the root.
distractor_rationales.At index n−1: Same as 'last index' — incorrect for same reason.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the role of the 'combine' step in divide-and-conquer algorithms?
choices: Merging sorted subarrays in merge sort
questions.correct_answer: Merging sorted subarrays in merge sort
questions.explanation: The 'combine' step integrates solutions of subproblems into a solution for the original problem — e.g., merging two sorted halves into one sorted array in merge sort.

distractor_rationales.Choosing the pivot in quicksort: Pivot selection is part of partitioning (the 'divide' step), not combining.
distractor_rationales.Recursively solving subproblems: This is the 'conquer' step — independent recursive calls on subproblems.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the failure function (also called LPS array) in the KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) string matching algorithm?
choices: To skip unnecessary character comparisons by leveraging prefix-suffix matches
To compute the hash value of each substring efficiently
To identify palindromic substrings in linear time
To build a suffix tree for the pattern
questions.correct_answer: To skip unnecessary character comparisons by leveraging prefix-suffix matches
questions.explanation: The LPS (Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix) array allows KMP to avoid backtracking in the text by determining how much of the pattern can be reused after a mismatch.

distractor_rationales.To compute the hash value of each substr: That describes rolling hash usage in Rabin-Karp, not KMP.
distractor_rationales.To identify palindromic substrings in li: That is the purpose of Manacher’s algorithm, not KMP.
distractor_rationales.To build a suffix tree for the pattern: Suffix trees are built via specialized algorithms (e.g., Ukkonen’s); KMP uses only a flat LPS array.

questions.prompt: What is the amortized time complexity per operation (find or union) in a union-find data structure with both union-by-rank and path compression?
questions.explanation: With union-by-rank and path compression, the amortized cost per operation is O(α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant for all practical input sizes.

distractor_rationales.O(1): While α(n) ≤ 4 for any n ≤ 2^65536, it is technically not constant — O(α(n)) is the precise bound.
distractor_rationales.O(log n): This is achievable with union-by-rank alone, but path compression improves it further.
distractor_rationales.O(n): This is far too pessimistic; even naive union-find is O(log n) with union-by-rank.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm is stable, in-place, and has worst-case time complexity O(n²)?
questions.explanation: Bubble sort is stable (does not swap equal elements out of order), in-place (uses only O(1) extra memory), and has O(n²) worst-case time.

distractor_rationales.Merge sort: Stable and O(n log n), but not in-place — requires O(n) auxiliary space.
distractor_rationales.Heap sort: In-place and O(n log n), but unstable — heap operations may reorder equal elements.
distractor_rationales.Quick sort: In-place and O(n²) worst-case, but unstable — partitioning swaps non-adjacent elements arbitrarily.
